1. Has the Government, or any member thereof, received the communication referred to in the following announcement, published in the the Sentinel of March 19, 1914? Collingwood Lodges Protest Against French
in Schools and on Post Cards and Government Stationery-Express Dissatisfaction with Local Representatives.
The brethren of L.O.L. Victoria No. 934, and Golden Lion No. 1990, Collingwood, at their regular meetings held on the 9th and 11th March, 1914, adopted the following resolution, and instructed their secretaries to forward same to the Orange Sentinel, to the Hon. R. L. Borden, Ottawa, and to the acting Premier, the Hon. J. J. Foy, Toronto, also to their representatives, Col. J. A. Currie, Ottawa, and Hon. Jas. Duff, Toronto:
Moved by Brother Wm. Elliot, P.M. L.O.L. 1990, seconded by Brother Peter McMillan, W.M. L.O.L. 943, and resolved:
That we, the members and officers of Victoria Lodge No. 943, and Golden Lion No. 1990, assembled at our regular meetings, take this opportunity of condemning in the strongest terms the action of the federal Government in permitting the issuance of the bilingual post cards, and the use of the French language upon the official stationery of the departments, and consider this departure an insult to the other nationalities, such as Germans, Highland Scotch and others, inasmuch as the English is the language of this country.
We also demand the immediate abolition of bilingual schools, as English must be the only language taught in our public schools, if we desire to grow up as a united body of citizens. And we do not uphold the attitude of our representatives in both Parliaments, as so far we have not noticed that they have taken any part, or raised their voices in opposing any of those encroachments, which is bound to be detrimental to the unity of this country.

The hon. member for St. John seemed to be deeply shocked a couple of days ago when he heard from the hon. member for South Renfrew that Mr. Gutelius was actually at one time in the

trusted employ of the Canadian Pacific railway, and that Mr. Lynch-Staunton was a Conservative. When Mr. Lynch-Staunton returned.

The hon. member for South Renfrew showed that he had been in communication with Mr. Parent and that Mr. Parent had complained to him about this very unjust treatment, but he never brought into the House a sentence or a word or a syllable to show that there had been the slightest error in the transcription of the notes of evidence in this report. The conclusion is irresistible-that the evidence was faithfully re-

ported and faithfully transcribed. If so, where is the injury?
The hon. member thinks that a very serious wrong was also done because this commission did not examine Mr. Charles Young on the question of the Winnipeg terminals. Having some knowledge of this subject myself, aside from the report, I was at a loss to understand what the reference of the hon. member for South Renfrew was as to the failure to take the evidence of Mr. Young. It will be remembered that in connection with the Winnipeg terminals the hon. member for South Renfrew said that whereas it was the first intention to bring the Transcontinental line into Winnipeg by connection at Dundee siding with the Canadian Northern, and running along the Canadian Northern into the joint terminals on the Winnipeg side of the. Red river, as a consequence of an investigation made personally by himself another route farther to the north was decided upon, and as a result the route of the road as now constructed was determined. It is quite true that the first route contemplated was a ground-level route, running alongside the Canadian Northern, and immediately to its north, or by the use of the Canadian Northern on a joint traffic basis.

My hon. friend, speaking from memory, has neglected to mention the whole of my statement in that respect. It was not only on account of a personal investigation I made that the present route was decided upon. My hon. friend will remember that I mentioned the fact that the Minister of Railways had the right to locate the route. I heard in my office the arguments of all companies and all those interested, and in addition to that I made a personal investigation. I would not like the country to think that it was only on a personal investigation made by myself that the route was decided upon.

I had no intention of leading the House to believe that it was only on account of my hon. friend's personal investigation that the decision was made. I know the hon. member did hear the interested parties; I know that as a consequence he came to the conclusion that the north route should be selected, that the wishes of the Canadian Pacific railway in that regard should be respected, and that the route should go just as it goes to-day, through a high-level line from St. Boniface across the Red river into the Winnipeg terminals. But what I want to draw attention to is, that the hon. member is

complaining that the commission had suppressed the evidence of Mr. Charles Young in their endeavour to show that due regard for economy was not observed in selecting this entrance in preference to the other. The hon. member must know, and he does know, that Mr. Charles Young was the commissioner who refused to consent to the selection of the ex-Minister of Railways himself, and that he was the only member of the commission who resisted, and continued to protest after the ex-Minister of Railways had come to his decision.
To be fair, the hon. gentleman should say that I mentioned that fact in my remarks.
I do not think the hon. gentleman did say that.
I said that Mr. Young dissented.

Then what had the commission to gain in making a point against the ex-Minister of Railways by suppressing the evidence of the one commissioner who resisted him? I do not think the hon. member for South Renfrew told the House at the time the decision was come to that the high-level entrance was not contemplated, and that afterwards when the high-level entrance was decided upon by the Railway Commission as being necessary, the consent of the engineer of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways to the adoption of that entrance was not secured.
The hon. member says it is all nonsense to complain of the Transcontinental Commissioners appointed by the Liberal Government because they were not practical railway men. Why, he says: we do not appoint practical railway men to run railways, we appoint any kind of .business men and these men take the advice of their engineers. Here is an instance where they did not take the advice of their engineers, but took the advice of the Minister of Railways himself, against that of the engineers, and adopted the high level entrance.
That is not the case.
Not the case?
No.
I had a lawsuit on this subject.
I hope my hon. friend won it.

What nonsense it is,
says the ex-minister, to suggest that the Liberal Government should appoint practical men, either in constructing or operating, to take charge of a great national undertaking. such as the building of a railway. He says: if you adopt that principle you are bound to have the Minister of Railways an engineer, either constructing or operating, and the Prime Minister of Canada as well. If his theory is correct, the Prime Minister of Canada would have to De master of every art and profession known to mankind. He says the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific railway do not appoint operating engineers to be heads of their railways; the Canadian Pacific railway did not do so when they appointed Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy, and so wre were quite justified in appointing a box manufacturer, a couple of lawyers, and a grain merchant from Delo-raine to'build the National Transcontinental railway. Can he give us an instance of the directors of the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern railway or of that wonderful road, the Union Pacific, or of any railway in the world, appointing as its president and general manager any one excepting a practical railwayman? Can he give us an instance in the whole history of railroad construction on this or any other continent where the directors or stockholders, responsible for the building of a railway, entrusted its building and its initial operation to men who were not practical railway men, either constructing or operating? There is no such instance in history. I do not believe he could imagine one instance in fiction, where any railway ever perpetrated the folly that the Liberal Government perpetrated when they appointed this commission to take charge of the .building of the National Transcontinental railway. I went to Winnipeg, said the hon. gentleman, I examined the surroundings, and I made up my mind that the National Transcontinental railway was not going to play second fiddle to the Canadian Northern railway or to any other road; I made up my mind that it was going to have an independent entrance of its own, and that there was going to he no second fiddle about it; that is the reason I adopted that north entrance. Let me picture to the hon. members of this House what that north entrance is. The railway comes in from Transcona, four and a half miles out. It crosses the Seine river and circles around until it gets to the Red river, through the flats of St. Boniface, which largely belong

to the Canadian Northern railway. It is built at an elevation of twenty-ijhree feet and presents a hideous spectacle from the city of Winnipeg or any other standpoint, being a tremendous embankment, lifting the railway into the air throughout the whole extent of its approach to Winnipeg. It goes over the Red river at high level; it reaches the joint terminals at high level, and the consequence is that where it should have some connection with the business element of Winnipeg, if it intends to get any business out of Winnipeg, it is almost as near the occupants of the heavens as it is to the people of Winnipeg. The road has a sky line through St. Boniface, and it cannot get a spur line connection with any business interests in the city of Winnipeg. How does the ex-minister expect the Transcontinental to get business out of Winnipeg? He has made a joint terminal arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway. The Canadian Northern railway own the	capital invested in
the	terminal,	and	except	over
lines owned by the Canadian Northern railway, the road cannot get a bit of freight out of Winnipeg. The hon. gentleman was very much afraid of making the Transcontinental play second fiddle to the Canadian Northern. What is that but having to play second fiddle to the Canadian Northern before they can get a ton of business out of that city? They have a connection whereby their trains must be pushed up to the high level line owned by the Transcontinental over a connecting link, which is the property of the Canadian Northern railway, and for the use of which the Transcontinental pays a certain rate of interest, and except over the line of the Canadian Northern railway and up to that connecting link, it cannot get business out of the city of Winnipeg. The hon. gentleman knows I am speaking correctly, he knows that is the only way they can get business there. They can get passenger business it is true out of the joint terminal, but they cannot get freight business, and they cannot connect with houses that would use the line as a freight line. Their whole terminal arrangement, their whole arrangement in Winnipeg even for passenger business, is to play second fiddle to the Canadian Northern railway. I was
aware, before the ex-Minister of Railways rose, and I think most of us were aware, that Mr. Staunton in that opinion did not agree with the Deputy Minister of Justice who gave the late Government his opinions and who gives this Government his opinions. It is as plain as anything could he, that when Mr. Hodgins made the very modest statement that these shops were built to amply take care of all future needs, he had in contemplation the needs of the Grand Trunk Pacific on the western line. Why do I say that? It is because Mr. Hodgins in his report, as quoted by the hon. member for South Renfrew, compares the facilities in these shops with the facilities of the

Canadian Pacific railway shops, and endeavours to show that in some respects they equal, or greatly exceed them, he evidently having in contemplation that the shops were to be used by both western and eastern lines just as Canadian Pacific shops are. I see he does not contradict me, but in case any one would like the evidence it ds to be found in ' Hansard,' July 11, 1908, page 12672, where Mr. Graham said:

But. I will tell the

hon. gentleman what we are not doing at Quebec, we are not spending money there for the Grand Trunk Pacific to use in connection with other lines they may own.

est during construction, which would come to $18,000,000, making a total of $181,000,000. That is correct, is it not?

He puts the cost at $4,500,000. (Reading):
What proportion of that would be fairly chargeable to this enterprise? I am going to assume that out of what it may cost we may fairly charge the Grand Trunk Pacific railway $2,000,000.
So that the Minister of Railways of the day, who himself fathered the whole scheme in this House of Commons, stated that about four-ninths of the cost of the Quebec bridge was properly chargeable to the Transcontinental. Four-ninths of the cost of the Quebec bridge is not quite the -same ais the armouries of this country; but what I want to draw my hon. friend's attention to is, that if we are to take what the cost of the Quebec bridge has been up to the present time, and its estimated cost for completion, and then take four-ninths of that as properly chargeable to the Transcontinental, we are going to add without interest at all, nearly $10,000,000 to the cost of the Transcontinental. On top of your $230,000,000, you have, on the authority of Mr. Fielding, to add that $10,000,000. On top of that also, you have to add interest for three years after the seven years, unless you are optimistic enough to think that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are going to find rental over working expenses for the three years. I do not believe that the ex-Minister of Railways in his heart of hearts would like to take as his share of the patrimony of this world, any part or all of the three years' rental we are going to get when the seven years are up. I do not think he would exchange it for his smallest possession in this world at the present time. If you add that three years' interest, and I think a sane regard for prospects will compel us to add it, you are going to add another $18,000,000 to the cost of the Transcontinental.
In all these calculations, which are sound, and which cannot be refuted, I have said noting at all about betterments until we get some return on the road. The ex-Minister of Railways knows that at the present hour the property of this country in the National Transcontinental, on the completed line not in use, or not in use to any serious extent, is depreciating day by day; that the Tails are rusting; that the ties are rotting; that the road bed is getting out of shape,

and that we shall have to spend huge sums of . money in betterments before we have as good a road as when it was first constructed. He says we are making up the $230,000,000 in such a way that if we applied the same plan to the Canadian Pacific railway, it would have cost $200,000,000 or $300,000,000. In that calculation the hon. gentleman took into account interest on the money advanced to the Canadian Pacific railway and on the land given to the Canadian Pacific railway at a cost of $5 an acre, compounded up to the present time.
I did not do that at all.
The hon. gentleman did do it in one calculation anyway.

In my calculation, on
which I computed the compound interest, there was no reference to the land at all; it was the cash given to the Canadian Pacific railway, and the value of the completed railway handed over to them at a valuation which in 1887 amounted, according to the figures in possession of the Government, to $72,000,000. I calculated cash and Toad completed, not land.
And he calculated interest on that up to the present time.
Yes.
If he takes the interest for a long enough period, he will make the amount anything he likes.

And, so can my hon.
friend in regard to the National Transcontinental railway.

In my opinion if you
compute interest, you should compute it up to the time when the country gets some service from the road.
Until the road is completed.

Well, who is objecting to that? What does the hon. member for St, John think about the method of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in calculating interest for thirty or forty years after the road is completed?
Then my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways went on to say that the capitalization of the road was quite reasonable, namely, $85,000 per mile, but if he calculates it at actual cost, plus interest, he is. going to get $99,500 a mile.

I did not say that.
Mr .MEIGHEN: I say that.

I said $85,000 a mile,
from Prince Rupert to Moncton. I took the figures given to me by the Government.
That is all right. I did not know that my hon. friend was referring to the road from coast to coast.
I was taking the whole road.

Well, we do not know what that road is going to cost yet; it is yet some distance from completion. At all events the National Transcontinental railway is the line which we are discussing and you cannot get its cost by mixing up the figures of another road. The National Transcontinental road will cost $99,500 a mile or almost $100,000 a mile for every mile of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton.

Does that include the
interest?

Without interest.

How much?

I am vety glad that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) interrupted me because I see that I was much too favourable to his side of the case. I gave $99,500 a mile as the cost with interest. In the moment or two of recess caused by the interruption, I find that the total cost of the road plus interest during construction alone aggregates $100,000 a mile.
By adding the computed interest for seven years, the cost pgr mile would amount to $117,000 instead of $99,500. My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) says that the road is worth it, because he says I can show you railroads in Germany that have cost more than that.

In speaking yesterday, I did not mention Germany directly or indirectly. In discussing railway matters here some years ago, I mentioned several railways in Europe. In my address of yesterday, taking the present Estimates, I mentioned the capitalization of four or five American roads, two of which I was giving for purposes of comparison. I did not mention any European roads at all.

I read in 'Hansard' a
reference by the hon. gentleman to Germany.
I did not say that.

I was not referring to my hon. friend's Sipeech of yesterday. But, at all events, I do not know what point the hon. member expects to make by interrupting me, for it is just the same whether it was in Germany, or in England or elsewhere. He referred to the Canadian Pacific railway, and to three or four roads in the thickly-populated parts of the United States-as if there were any comparison 'between land values in the state of New York and land values at Graham, Redditt, Cochrane, Fitzpatrick and various other points in our yet unpeopled north. His method is to put the cost of this bare line of railway against the Canadian Pacific railway, with its telephone system, its telegraph system, its hotels, its lands, its steamships, and all its other multifarious assets.
Now the hon. gentleman says: Whatever it cost, it is worth the money. And that is the report we always get when we present the case of the people of Canada against the late Government for unneces-

sarily adding to the cost of the Transcontinental. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: Whatever it cost, and whatever blunders we made, whether in the agreement or after the agreement, or in the execution of the work, we put those blunders behind our backs and under our feet, because the road is worth the money anyway.
Well, the feature of the case I wish to present, with what emphasis I may, is just that in estimating the money that ' should be spent on a railroad, whether in whole or in part, some regard should be had to reasonable expectations of traffic for the years after the road is completed. And, however optimistic hon. gentlemen may be of the traffic that will go over this road, their optimism does not justify us in flinging reason and discretion to the winds and assuming that on the Transcontinental railway, immediately after construction or very shortly after construction, we can have a traffic comparable with the present traffic on the Canadian Pacific railway. It is pointed out in this report, and not refuted even by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., so far as I am informed, that the equating tables presented to the engineers of this road, as they located the same and laid it out, were based upon the hypothesis that the road, as soon as it was open for traffic, [DOT]would receive a traffic double that of the present traffic on the Canadian Pacific Tailway. And these equating tables, calculated for the purpose of showing under what circumstances it would pay to make capital investment rather than incur expense for operation, were based upon a hypothesis which no reasonable man would be justified in holding. As a consequence of this hypothesis, twhich violates every principle of discretion and common sense, the road was laid out and constructed at a cost that defeats the very purpose for which the road was projected. The hon. member for South Renfrew read some letters to show that because in this construction they had got down to a better grade than another transcontinental line, they could carry traffic much cheaper; he went on to show that the Transcontinental railway could carry wheat, I think he said, for about one-third the rate the Canadian Pacific railway could carry it for, and almost as cheaply as it could be carried by water. But no sooner was this said than the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) asked: What about the obligation

of the company to pay rental on this tremendous capitalization as affecting their ability to make loiw traffic rates? And the hon. gentleman's answer was: I will tell the hon. member later on. But he has not told him about that rental yet; he has never admitted, in figuring the cost to the Transcontinental, the interest on the capitalization, which must be taken into account in arriving at the rates which that railway will be able to give its customers.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. 'member undrlly, but I would refer him to page 2107 of ' Hansard ' on that point. I know the hon. member was not here last night, and I am sure he has not read this or he would not make the statement he does. I gave the statement as to what it would cost to operate this line, taking the expected traffic as given by Mr. Tye before this commission. My hon. friend will see that I put in the cost of operation as one of the charges, the very amount figured out by the commission as rental:
Interest charges per day,' as per commissioners report, $14,800.
So, I answered the hon. member for St. Antoine as I promised.
Does the hon. member for a moment suggest that in his cost of operation he has included overhead charges?
The hon. gentleman said I did not mention that. If he will follow out what I said he will see that there was a balance left to pay all other expenses.

Very well, but what I
said was that the hon. member did not include the cost of rental in order to arrive at what the traffic would cost, and when he does include the rental he leaves out interest. The hon. gentleman admits that.
I do not.

Then, I do not understand what he says. The hon. gentleman dwelt at great length on the question of grades, and he set about to convince the House that he was quite justified, and that the Transcontinental railway commissioners were quite justified, in entirely eliminating from thisToad what are known as momentum grades, and the Gutelius-Staunton report is entirely in error when it informs the people of Canada that $6,200,000 was thrown to the winds in this effort to do away entirely with the possibility of momentum grades. The hon. gentleman quoted letter after letter to show that the better grade you can get on a railway the cheaper you

can carry the traffic. Nobody disputes that general proposition. But still you have to keep in mind the cost of construction, and the interest on that cost if you arc going to be fair in your calculations. But that is what the hon. gentleman did not do: that is what the eengineers of the Transcontinental were forbidden to do. That is why we have a cost of construction that defeats the very purpose of the road.
Hon. gentlemen opposite would convince us that momentum grades are fearful things. One would actually think, to hear the hon. gentleman describe them, that a train on a road on which there were momentum grades, would rock about like an automobile on a rough road, and that momentum grades were dangerous not only to the lives of those who rode over them but to the country through which the train passes.
Hear, hear.

It is well that we should grasp what momentum grades really mean.
I understand that the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) agrees with me in my description. Let me illustrate to the right hon. gentleman just how much truth there is in his belief. The momentum grades that have been allowed in the interest of economy on the Transcontinental have a maximum depth of eight feet; but the momentum grades on the Canadian Pacific railway between here and Carleton Place have a maximum depth of thirty feet. The right hon. gentleman himself has travelled over this Canadian Pacific line many times, and I do not think he has suffered very serious turmoil to his anatomy.
Now, what are these momentum grades?
Will the hon. gentleman tell the House where the momentum grades on the Transcontinental are? I have not been able to get that information so far.

I have a list of them here, but I do not think the right hon. gentleman would be very much edified if I were to read to the House about 1,000 figures. I shall be glad to send the list over to him. I understand that it was brought down in response to an order for a return to this House, but I may be misinformed as to that.

I have not
seen them.	*	.

What are these momentum grades? The ruling gradient on the Transcontinental is 0.4 per cent as against
eastbound traffic, and 0.6 per cent as against westbound traffic. Those were the grades determined upon, and they were determined upon without any reference to the character of the country through which the road was to be run, and without any reference to whether or not such construction would be in the interests of the road or would help fulfil the purposes of the road. Apparently the cost of the road was not considered in its relation to the rates to be charged on the freight that might be carried over it. The cardinal blunder in connection with putting into execution the design of the Government in connection with the Transcontinental was in heeding not in the slightest degree the necessity of keeping the capital cost down to a minimum, in the interests of the road itself. No attention, then, was paid to the equating tables. The engineers were told to make 0.4 per cent and 0.6 per cent grades and to have no momentum grades, no matter what the result might be. The consequence is that the interest charges on the road are so high that there is no hope whatever of securing low freight rates, which the road was built to secure. It would appear from the speech of the hon. member for South Renfrew that the moment you introduce a momentum grade you depart entirely from the four-tenths and six-tenths actual grade. You will do nothing of the kind. A four-tenths grade, if I understand it aright, means that there is at no place a greater rise than four-tenths of a foot in one hundred feet against eastbound traffic, and in no case a greater rise than six-tenths of a foot in one hundred feet against westbound traffic. Consequently, an engine of certain power can haul a train loaded to a certain capacity over that four-tenths grade east-bound and six-tenths grade westbound and, if the momentum grades that are introduced are really momentum grades in the real meaning of the term, 5 p.m. they in no way interfere with the power of an engine to carry exactly the same load over exactly the same route. One would think that you limit the hauling capacity of your engine, the moment you introduce a momentum grade, no matter how slight, and that, at no matter what cost, such grades ought to be eliminated. Momentum grades, the hon. gentleman says, are of very doubtful advantage. He tells us that a momentum grade is of value to the road; at least he says it does not do it any harm. I admit

that it does not do any harm, but the question of cost comes into the construction of a non-momentum railroad. It 'becomes a question how much you should pay to produce a non-momentum system. The hon. gentleman refused to let that question intervene at all; to him it did not matter what it cost. Ordinary business sense should have dictated to him to ascertain first of all whether a non-momentum road is any better than a momentum road for the traffic that this line is expected to carry, and, if you ascertain that it is better, then find out whether it is so much better that it warrants the paying of $6,200,000 for it. Surely that is a matter of ordinary business; but the hon. gentleman did not do that. The momentum grade means this: you carry the very same load with the very same power. By means of a down-grade for a short distance and upgrade the rest, the momentum that the train secures going down carries it up the other side,, and as a result the principle of momentum is introduced and a great saving is effected without any detraction from the operating value of the road. The principle is not that of degrading the road to introduce momentum grades. The hon. gentleman has scoured the continent of America in order to produce the opinion of an engineer, if he could get one, that momentum grades should never be introduced. He scoured the continent of America and the continent of Europe ffi prove to this House that under no circumstances should momentum grades be used on the National Transcontinental railway. Having done this-and he has had seven or eight years in which to do it-he has not, in a speech lasting seven hours and a half, produced a single witness to show to this House that momentum grades should not be introduced. He could not and did not quote a line from either Mr. Berry or Mr. Cooper, one an engineer from the southern States and one from England, to show that momentum grades should not be used on the Transcontinental. He went to the American Association of Engineers, but the report of that association, from which In quoted, showed that he was wrong, and that there were circumstances under which momentum grades undoubtedly ought to be introduced in the interests of the road it-itself.

I have always admitted that there are circumstances under which momentum grades are practicable. I never

suggested anything else, but they are not practicable in a frost and snow country.
Not in a cold country?
I said a frost and snow country.

The hon. gentleman's
opinion is that momentum grades are all right under perfect circumstances, but that they are not all right in a frost and snow country.
On new lines.

Here is the opinion of
one of the engineers quoted by my hon. friend-and I venture to say it was the most in his favour of any that he could secure from the whole report:
Modern railroad practice has substantially established the fact that momentum grades have their uses and are frequently of great value, but there are definite and well-known objections to their indiscriminate use.
Who would not know that?
And that they should be adopted as a matter of course ordinarily or wherever opportunity offers, especially in original locations, may be seriously questioned.
Hear, hear.

Does the Gutelius-
Staunton report say in a single instance that momentum grades should be indiscriminately applied, or wherever opportunity offered? All Gutelius and Staunton said in the report was exactly what the American Association said in the report quoted by my hon. friend. The view of the association was:
Modern railroad practice has substantially established the fact that momentum grades have their uses and are frequently of great value.
But the Transcontinental railway proceeded on the presumption that modern railway practice had established the fact that there was no value in momentum grades at all.
The hon. gentleman went down to the southern .States and produced Mr. Berry, whose reputation is said to be international, but whom I never heard of before, although I have heard of many American engineers whose reputations became international very suddenly. However, I will accept Mr. Berry's opinion as that of an engineer of international reputation. In all the quotations which the hon. gentleman made from Mr. Berry, he cannot point to a line wherein Mr. Berry states that momentum grades

should not have been applied to the Tran -continental railway.
Mr. Berry was asked by the hon. gentleman himself to be a witness on this matter. I do not know whether Mr. Berry ever read the evidence. I have not seen the letter which the hon. gentleman wrote to him. I do not think he read the evidence, because he does not refer to it. But this gentleman from South America-
Not South America.

The southern States- does say that there are circumstances when momentum grades should not be used, and he makes it as clear as day that there should always be an equation made between the advantage to be gained by momentum grades and the possible disadvantage. He thinks non-momentum grades are worth getting if you get them cheaply enough. Consequently he says there is a doubt amongst railway engineers whether or not a momentum grade is better than a non-momentum grade, and therefore, says my hon. friend (Mr. Graham), we are ready to pay any sum to remove the doubt. Whoever heard of reasoning tike- that. Mr. Berry almost says, and the ex-Minister of Railways does say, that you dare not have momentum grades in a cold country where there is snow and frost; and I wish to follow Mr. Berry and see just how far he establishes the point. Mr. Berry, in the course of his letter, points out that there are certain circumstances where a momentum grade may interfere with operating. He said that in the case of the momentum grade shown in the report, which was put there for the purpose of illustration, if you started out a fully loaded train of empties at the top of that momentum grade it would not get up the other side. There is his first objection. Whoever heard of putting in a momentum grade where you would be starting a fully loaded train of empties at the top? Would not a fully loaded train of empties, if that momentum grade was located in the only sensible place where any man would locate it, have a speed of ten or twenty miles an hour when it Teached the foot of the down grade, and in that case it would get up the other side just as any other train would. That is what momentum means. Who would start a train over a momentum grade without iany head at the top of the momentum? But he says a still more terrible thing might happen in a cold country of thirty degrees below zero. Mr. Berry says that if you strike a momentum
grade in a cold country, thirty degrees below zero, with five inches of snow on the rails, and if, when you get to the bottom of the grade your engine goes up the spout, then you will not get to the top. Those are the only two circumstances that the ingenious mind of Mr. Berry can devise in order to show that you should never have a momentum grade in order to insure the country against the calamitous result of a train of empties started at the top of a momentum grade without any momentum and getting stalled before it gets to the-other side, and the still more calamitous result of a fully loaded train of cars, at thirty degrees below zero and with five inches of snow on the rails getting stuck at the bottom through a dead engine, we ought to spend $6,200,000 of the money of the people of Canada. He cannot point to me in Mr. Berry's report a single other instance, a single other possibility that Mr. Berry's ingenious mind can devise that would defeat the real purpose of momentum grades. I read a few minutes ago what the hon. gentleman quoted from the report of the* American Railway Engineering and Maintenance of Way Association. Just bear with me while I quote that again in order that I may show you the reasoning of the ex-Minister of Railways. Here lis the quotation he made:
Modern railroad practice has substantially established the fact that momentum grades have their uses and are frequently of great value, but there are definite and well-known objections to their indiscriminate use, and that they should be adopted as a matter of course ordinarily or wherever opportunity offers, especially in original location, may be seriously questioned.
Now let me give you the deduction which the logical mind of the hon. member for South Renfrew draws from that statement:
This association takes the ground that even where the conditions are perfect, it is a mistake to introduce velocity grades-
Go on.

-
On a new line.
Hear, hear. That makes a difference.

The hon. gentleman says 'hear, hear.' The Maintenance of Way Association said:
There are definite and well-known objections to their indiscriminate use and that they should be adopted as a matter of course ordinarily or wherever opportunity offers, especially in original location, may be seriously questioned.
Hear, hear.

It may be questioned
whether you can adopt them indiscriminately or whenever opportunity offers, no matter what the result to be gained is, under those circumstances, in original construction. That is what the Maintenance of Way Association says. The deduction of the Minister of Railways is that unless conditions are perfect it is a mistake to introduce velocity grades.
My hon. friend has left out again the word ' on a new line'.
On a new line.
That makes a difference.

Does the hon. member say that the Maintenance of Way Association said that? They said that on new lines it may be questioned whether you should introduce them indiscriminately or ordinarily or wherever opportunity offers.
Hear, hear.

Nobody would say anything else on new lines. This association says that you should use due care in the introduction of momentum grades. You would not introduce them, for instance, at a divisional point where you are going to start a train of empties at the foot of a momentum grade without any momentum. That would be their use indiscriminately, and ordinarily, and wherever opportunity offered. The Maintenance of Way Association say that you should not do that, but that is a long way from saying that you should never do it on a new line at all. It is just the difference between doing it without discrimination and doing it with discrimination. The hon. member for South Renfrew does not see that difference and the reason he gives is:
For you do not know where the density of traffic is going to he and you cannot establish the velocity grades in the proper places.
That hon. gentleman says, that because we do not know, for example, what the traffic is going to be between Winnipeg and Lake Superior Junction, we do not know where the density is going to be along the Jine. such great density that you would not dare have momentum grades of that kind, at whatever cost he is going to abolish momentum grades altogether. Doe3 the hon. gentleman fear a traffic along that line so great that you could not have momentum grades? The Canadian Pacific railway do not fear it. The Canadian Pacific railway have been running their line between Fort William and Winnipeg 
until now they have a double track, and on the revision of their line, knowing full well the traffic and having due regard for the future traffic, I have the evidence and the proof here to show that they have 85 momentum grades of importance on that line between Winnipeg and Fort William, or a momentum grade for about every three or four miles of the road.
But my hon. friend is fearful that we are going to have such a congestion of traffic between Lake Superior Junction and the city of Winnipeg that it would be a fatal thing to introduce a momentum grade at all. I have a letter here from an engineer who has the confidence of hon. gentlemen opposite. He was employed by them on the Transcontinental-or, perhaps not by them-at all events he was employed on the Transcontinental. He is an eminent engineer who made an inspection of the profiles of the Canadian Pacific railway at my own request. He writes:
The ruling grade, that is the maximum grade when neither momentum or pusher grades are used, between these points is, according to the information given me, 0.4 per cent against both east and westbound. This information checks with the profiles.
The momentum grades are not used to the same extent against eastbound as against westbound traffic as regards the rate of grade but there are probably about the same number of them each way. I counted 85 in all, and left out quite a number of the lighter ones. The rate of grade varies against eastbound from 0.5 per cent, 0.6 per cent, 0.7 per cent, 0.8 per cent to 0.9 per cent and in one ease 1.0 per cent. Against westbound traffic the rate varies also from 0.5 per cent to 1.2 per cent, there being numerous cases of over 1.0 per cent. X noticed in a few cases that these grades were used in such a way as I would hesitate to adopt myself because of the high rates of speed required.
If we leave out the 40 miles west from Fort William and 60 miles east from Winnipeg, the average of these grades for the remaining distance is roughly one to every four miles. In one section of 22 miles, however, I found 13 momentum grades with a more frequent use of the higher rates of grade, there being three cases of the use of 0.8 per cent against eastbound and 1.0, 1.15 and 1.3 per cent against westbound.
That is the judgment of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; and they have lately revised their line and deemed it in the interest of the company and the purposes the railway was built to serve that they should introduce these momentum grades because of the great cost of obviating them. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) says: 'If you look at the time sheets of that company, you will find that where there are momentum grades on a ruling grade of 0 4 per cent,. they do not

load their trains to capacity. I understand the time sheets do not say anything about it.

I did not say time sheets.
I said weigh sheets. Perhaps that is not the proper term, but the sheet I mean shows the loading of the trains.

At the time Mr. Grant
made that report as to momentum grades, he was not chief engineer.
Did the hon. gentleman take his advice as to momentum grades after be was chief engineer?

I do not think my hon. friend will find that Mr. Grant, except in one or two instances, gave advice as to momentum grades. Grant did not pretend to be chief engineer at the time he wrote that report; lie got his orders from the chief engineer.

He got his orders from Ottawa, he says. But did the hon. gentleman take his advice as to momentum grades after he became chief engineer? In twc most important instances the hon. gentle-

man took his own opinion instead of that of his chief engineer.
The evidence is on file to show that the chief engineer before him was overpowered from Ottawa and that he was not allowed to exercise his own best judgment by this Transcontinental Railway Commission. and the Minister of Railways and Canals. As a result finally of being impeded in the fair discharge of his duties by these orders from Ottawa, he threw up his post as chief engineer and retired from the service altogether.

Mr. Grant did not do
that.

Mr. Grant took his *orders from Ottawa, Mr. Grant did it against his best judgment and on account of being compelled to do it he was made a party to the extraction from the treasury [DOT]of this country of $6,200,000 which is chargeable to the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Now, the hon. member for South Renfrew says that he is afraid of the snow and the ice of this country, and that therefore he refused to sanction momentum grades. Did he ever ask the chief engineer about snow and ice? Did he ever ask him if this gentleman from the southern States-
No, Chicago; get it right.
From Omaha.
No.

I think I am right when I mention Omaha because he reduced the grades of the Union Pacific. My information is that he did reduce the grades of the Union Pacific, but that he reduced them from two and a half per cent down to one per cent. That was the revision on the Union Pacific grades, and if you have a reduction of gradients to one per cent there is not so much need of introducing momentum grades as there is if you get down to 0.4 per cent or 0.3 per cent. It is then that the momentum grade is imperative in the interest of common sense and economy because you have not as much latitude in locating and constructing your line as you have with a one per cent grade. Momentum grades are introduced not when the gradient is high but when the gradient is low. If the gradient is high you can get [DOT]economy without the momentum grade, but if the gradient is low you cannot.

Then why did the hon. gentleman say that the momentum grade is

used on the Canadian Pacific railway, when the Canadian Pacific railway has a grade of over 0.4 per cent?
Because, in the revision of their grade, they reduced the gradients.

By the momentum
grade?

It is when you get a
0.4 per cent grade that you want momentum grades. When the Canadian Pacific were getting their 0.4 per cent grade the momentum grade was regarded as an economic consideration and one in the interest of the road. But when the Transcontinental Railway Commission were getting a 0.4 per cent grade they flung economy and common sense to the winds. That is the difference between the Transcontinental and the Canadian Pacific railway.
As to this engineer from Omaha who reduced the grade of the Union Pacific from two and a half to one per cent. This is the engineer from the southern States who writes up to the Canadian people and tells them that the Laurentian and granite rocks in this northern country which have withstood the elements for ages, will be disintegrated beyond all recognition if exposed to rain and ice. That is the suggestion he makes with reference to the granite of northern Canada. The enigma has so frightened the hon. member for South Renfrew that he says that momentum grades are going to interfere so much, under conditions of snow and ice and frost, with the operation of the road and are going to impede trains to such an extent that it would not be right to introduce them. had to do with the great, successful railways of this country, rather than the opinion of a man from Omaha on the question of snow and ice. Here is what Mr. Grant says in a letter addressed to me on the 25th March:

M. P. and J. T. Davis. The contract price was a huge figure, running up into the millions, and at the time the contract was let the conditions 'were such that whoever tendered on it would find very great difficulty in reaching the scene of their labours and getting their supplies and tlheir men there. As a consequence, it must have been contemplated that the tenders that would be received in answer to the advertisement would be more than ordinarily high. The tenders were more than ordinarily high. The reasons for the high tenders doubtless were the inaccessibility of the locality and the difficulty that would be encountered in getting supplies and men to the scene. Section 8. The said work shall he commenced immediately after the execution of this agreement and shall he proceeded with continuously and diligently, and under the personal supervision of the contractor, until completed.
Was lit commenced immediately? Was it carried on with diligence, or in any other way? It was not. So that clause of the contract undoubtedly was violated. Then further:
Section 20. In case the contractor shall make default or delay in diligently continuing to execute or advance the works to the satisfaction of the engineer, and such default or delay shall continue for six days after notice in writing shall have been given hy the engineer to the contractor requiring him to put an end to such default or delay, or in case the contractor shall become insolvent . . . the commissioners may take the work out of the hands of the contractor.

P. and J. T. Davis from that contract. a month; and they did it at the request of the head of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company who themselves were contractors and who stood to lose if that penalty were exacted. In order to find out whether it was the duty of the late Government to call for that $5,000 a month, to whom did they write?
They wrote to Mr. Hays, President of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, which company themselves were contractors for 353 miles of the line; which company themselves were in default and liable to the $5,000 penalty. That is where they went for advice. I have here a certified copy of the resolution which was passed by the Transcontinental Railway Commission. It reads:

Mr. Speaker, I can conclude all I have to say on the subject of contracts by a reference to the discussion that has so far preceded in regard to subletting. It will be recalled that the report of this commission finds that as nearly as may be estimated, some $8,800,000 has been lost to the country by means of injudicious advertising and injudicious restrictions in the matter of the letting of the contracts. That was assumed by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken as a finding on the part of the commission that the whole principle of sub-letting was a vicious principle, and that it was not in the public interest. The commissioners were attacked in the severest terms of censure because they had attacked the principle of sub-letting, and the Government of to-day is charged with having no faith in that commission and with violating its findings because they absolutely countenanced sub-letting on the Hudson bay railway and the Welland canal. I have not been able to find any assertion in the report of the commission that there is anything inherently wrong in the principle of sub-letting. Nobody objects to the principle of sub-letting properly applied, the public interest being safeguarded. But is it only sub-letting that has taken place here on the Transcontinental railway? It is not sub-letting at all, in the main it is selling of the contracts; it is securing something under conditions that shut out competition, and, having secured it, turning it over to somebody who does the work that the primary contractor should have done, at an immense profit. For example, the sale of the Davis contract is not a sub-letting. O'Brien, Fowler and Mac-dougall Bros, may have sub-let afterwards. That is very frequently done. The contractors first sold, then the man who purchased from them sub-let, and perhaps two or three under him got contracts. Then they would sub-let again, and so on. All that has taken place under the conditions stipulated by the late Transcontinental commission. What was one condition that was severely to be criticised? The commission advertised for tenders and called for a certain deposit with the tender. But they inserted in their advertisement a provision that, not only did they require that deposit, but that they reserved to themselves the right to demand any further sum whatever, within a certain number of days; and unless this sum was put up, not only would the man who tendered be in danger of losing the contract, although he might be the lowest tenderer, but he would face the probability of losing his cash deposit. In other words, he delivered himself bodily into the hands of the com-

mission, because the commission might exact from him something which he could not possibly comply with. Surely no hon. gentleman opposite will say that this was not such a restriction as was calculated to shut out competition. I am at a loss to imagine what other purpose such a restriction could have had, or what the commission could have had in mind were it not to shut out competition in reserving to themselves the right to practically ruin the tenderer if he did not comply with conditions that in advance he knew nothing of. The clause to which I refer is as follows:
And I hereby declare and agree that in case of refusal or failure to execute the said contract with the commissioners and also to furnish the approved security required-[DOT]
Not knowing what it was.
-to an amount not exceeding one-third of the estimated total consideration of the contract, for the faithful performance of the said contract, within ten days after the acceptance of this tender, the said cheque shall he forfeit to the said commissioners as liquidative damages for such failure, and all contract rights secured by the acceptance of this tender shall be forfeited.
The checks demanded varied in amount from 575,000 to 5400,000, and the subsequent security varied from nothing up to about $1,300,000 in the case of the McArthur contract. But the point is that the contractor had no possible conception, except that he was limited to one-third of the whole contract price, as to what he might be called upon to do. If that were a justifiable proceeding in this case is it not in all Government contracts? Why is an exception made in the case of the Transcontinental Commission and their contracts? The Minister of Finance of that day saw that the effect of regulations that the Transcontinental Commission had put into effect, in this restrictive clause, inevitably would be to so discourage prospective tenderers as to limit very seriously their number and consequently to enhance very materially the cost. He wrote a letter of protest, asking that the commission should recede from that position and should be content with such conditions as prevailed in other Government contracts. But his request was not heeded and the Government of the day did not see to it that fair and reasonable conditions only were insisted upon, and in that way at least one element of cost eliminated. They decided in this case, just as in every other case, whenever a question was before them on one side of

which was a reduction of cost and on the other side an increase of cost, they decided every time on the extra expenditure, whatever it might be. Was there ever a question or dispute that reached the commission, or, above the commission, reached the Government, that was not decided in favour of the extra expense? So that the' attack on the system of advertising and tendering and the consequences of that system is not an attack on sub-letting as sub-letting, and all that the commission say is that one step in the process at least might have been eliminated, there might have been one clause struck out and one element of the cost prevented if a fair system had been adopted. In that way they estimate that $8,800,000 was wasted. The basis of this estimate is only a fair average between the first cost and the second cost, not between the first cost and the actual cost to the men who-performed the work.
I have not yet dealt with the question of curvature. It is very much akin to the question of momentum grades. On the question of momentum grades I think it has been clearly established that a loss to this country of $6,200,000 has resulted; and in estimating that loss regard has only been had to what could have been saved after the line of railway was decided upon. If this stringent condition had not been laid down before the line was decided upon, a line of railway would have been laid out on which there could have been saved a great deal more than $6,200,000. The commission were not in a position to say what might have been done unless they went to work and laid out a different line altogether. They could only say what could have been saved with the line of railway as it is, had it not been determined that, come what might, and at whatever cost, momentum grades were to be absolutely debarred. As to curvature the very same words, in effect, apply. They determined in advance, without any regard to the topography of the country, and having no interest at all in what the result to the country might be of their determination-they determined in advance on a 6 degree curve as the maximum, no matter what the cost of that 6 degree might be to the country. The hon. member for South Renfrew says the curvature is as important as the grade, because if you increase the curvature you produce exactly the same result in retarding operation as if you increase the grade. That is very true. And he says, if you have an 0.4 per cent grade and then add

10 degr&es curvature, you are doubling the 0 4 per cent grade; and the conclusion that might be very reasonably drawn from that is that you cannot afford to add a maximum curvature to the maximum gradient. That is to say, the conclusion .put generally is this: That in curvature just as in gradients you cannot indiscriminately apply the maximum. You have to use judgment, take into account all the conditions surrounding each case, and decide each one on its merits. That is all that the commission report asked for. What is there in the argument of the hon. member for South Renfrew as against this proposition, that where the road is on the level it (would not have been advisable to have used a 10 degree curvature instead of a 6 degree, even if a large saving might have been made thereby. Ten degrees curvature on the level is equal to 0-4 per cent grade. You are not in any way diminishing the hauling power of an engine: the engine could take just the same load as df that 10 degree curve were not there, but they had no regard whatever for this consideration, and just because it would cost more in all cases to have a 6 degree curve, they insisted upon it. They appear to have acted on the principle that the greater the cost the better for Canada, and in all cases they decided on the greater cost irrespective of the merits of the particular case in hand.
It is a fact established by the evidence, and which the hon. member for South Renfrew will not deny, that the 10 degree curve is used on all the important railways m this country. It is the best in the judgment of the Canadian Pacific railway and other roads, and surely the judgment of successful Canadian roads is the judgment that we would be wise in following.
It is said by the expert from Omaha that the commissioners just made a wild guess in getting at $602,000 as the saving that would be effected if they had gone as far and no further than a 10 degree curve on this road, without in any degree diminishing the hauling capacity of the engines or the operating value of the road. I do not know upon what Mr. Berry bases his remark. The commission assert that they went thoroughly into it. They took the evidence, and I have before me a statement showing every detail by which this $602,000 was arrived at for one-quarter of the line; and inasmuch a3 the rest of the line hears a fair comparison with this one-quarter of the line in this regard, I think four times that is what the commission would be expected to arrive at as the saving on the whole line. I would like to place the figures on 'Hansard,' if I may do so.

At all events, he left out a very important element of cost, and I want to point out that the annual rental from Winnipeg to Quebec is about $4,200,000. On the basis of calculation of

On 50,000,000 bushels pf wheat which, compared with the other traffic, would be a very large computation, and I do not think we could add everything else in and possibly hope to exceed that, you will have to get eight cents a bushel to pay the rental and then you have to pay the whole cost of operation and overhead expenses on top of that.
Does my hon. friend not think it fair to admit that there will be something drawn besides wheat?
Yes, but I do not admit that there will be 50,000,000 bushels of wheat.
No, and there will not have to !be.

If the whole import of the United Kingdom is 260,000,000 bushels, how can we expect to get 50,000,000 bushels for the Transcontinental, 50,000,000 bushels for the Canadian Northern railway and from
75.000.	000 to 100,000,000 bushels for the Canadian Pacific railway? To do that we will have to control the whole of the wheat from the rest of the world. So, I say, taking everything reasonable into consideration, it would require a traffic that would be fairly represented by 50,000,000 bushels

of wheat, at eight cents a bushel to pay the rental alone.
If you did not draw anything else.

The hon. gentleman
himself left out passenger traffic. It is impossible to estimate everything. Does the hon. gentleman believe that the whole traffic will exceed a traffic represented by
50,000,000 bushels of wheat?

It would probably exceed the traffic that would he represented by half of 50,000,000 bushels of wheat anyway. The fallacy that my hon. friend is falling into is that the rate on grain is very low but the rate on manufactured goods going back, and goods coming from the old land, is much higher and you have to calculate that you will get as great returns from the other traffic as from the wheat.
I do not think that is the case. I do not think that the hon. gentleman will say that it is the experience of other roads that they get anything like the traffic in that they get out. "
Not in tonnage, but returns in money.

Or returns. I remember the hon. gentleman's remarks on another subject, a subject that I really thought he would be correct on if he could be correct on anything. He objected very strenuously to the evidence of Mr. Tompkins and to the conclusion from the evidence that there had been a huge loss in the construction of engine houses. It will be remembered that Mr. Thomas Tompkins was the witness who gave evidence to a man of practical experience that the fortunate gentlemen who, under the peculiar system of the commission, got the building of these engine houses, out of a total cost of $203,911.78, had been able to pocket in profit $115,209.19. They had secured over 50 per cent, or more than half of the whole cost as profit. That was the finding of Mr. Tompkins. My hon. friend said that Mr. Tompkins was not a good authority on the subject. He said that he was an old friend of his down in Brockville, that he had known him quite well some fifteen or twenty years ago when he did know something about building engine houses, but that he had forgotten all about it, just as my hon. friend has forgotten how to set type. I am afraid the hon. gentleman has not followed the career of this gentleman very closely. I took occasion to make inquiries with reference to this matter far-
[Mr. Meighen.l
ther, and ascertained that Mr. Tompkins was the man who built the engine houses for the Canadian Pacific railway at Cliap-leau and at Westmount dn 1906, and that he was the man who had been the most recent constructor of engine houses in Canada, and who had built them actually about the time that the engine houses were built on the Grand Trunk Pacific. Mr. Gutelius having known his friend (he having built engines under him), and knowing that he was actually engaged in the same work at approximately the very same time, I think my hon. friend will have to admit that no better witness could have been secured. The hon. gentleman has now to defend the process of letting contracts that gave the contractors $115,000 of profit out of a $203,000 job.
There is another phase of the subject that I want to speak of now, namely, the subject of trestles and, in connection with that, the subject of over-break. The hon. gentleman has a very poor opinion of wooden trestles. He thinks that they are going to rot, and consequently they never should be put up. We all know that wooden trestles, or wooden anything else, will not last forever. We all know that in their nature they are more or less temporary. No one has ever disputed that, but the question that is before us is this: Was it in the interest of good business, in the interest of ths railway and dn the interest of the country that wooden trestles be put there for the same purpose that wooden trestles are put on every other road? That is the question before us. Wooden trestles are used for two purposes. Where they require, or desire, to have a train fill over a valley, wooden trestles of a very temporary character are used, dn order that the small donkey engines of the contractor may go over them and in that way dump the loads of earth into the fill. That is only one purpose. They are not used very much for that purpose, but there is another. Wooden trestles are used on all roads in order that a temporary structure may be used for such valleys as I have mentioned, where a train fill, or cement or steel structures are ultimately intended, in order that we may provide more cheaply in the end for the ultimate character of the construction intended and in order that the trains may carry the filling over the line and that the filling may be dumped into these structures as time goes on. The hon. gentleman says that that is a very poor system because there is danger of fire-

and no doubt there is some little danger of fire. He says that on account of that danger a little will be added to the cost of operation, but he has made no calculation to show that the danger of fire and the consequent cost of guarding against it bear any relation whatever to the saving that would have accrued if this system had been adopted. He simply tells us that we cannot adopt it, no matter what the saving may be. The privileges that ordinary railway companies have are denied to this Government in the building of a railway. It may be that the Grand Trunk Pacific would use this system in their western line. He assumed that they did use it. He admitted that they built wooden trestles wherever it would pay them to do so, and when they had no barrier to prevent them doing so. He knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific railway in western Canada, ever since their line has been constructed, and that is many years ago, has used wooden trestles and are 'using wooden trestles still. There are large and long structures of wooden trestles right in Manitoba, and that road has been operated over them for years, and doubtless will be operated over them for some time to come. Why should not the same system of building have been adopted here, inasmuch as it is in the interest of economy, and without in any way detracting from the value of the road? Why is it that the Government of Canada was debarred, as the hon. gentleman says they were, from adopting any system of economy that was in the interest of the road and of the. country, and that was open to any other railway company to adopt? My hon. friend says, we could not do that, for if we did the Grand Trunk Pacific would not take over the road. We have bound ourselves, he says, to deliver over to them a railway actually completed and ready for operation. Well, Mr. Fielding, his predecessor in charge of this work, did not take that view. He, as shown by the report, very clearly took the view that the same course was open to the then Government as was open to any other builder of a railway, and that they could build a road which would save money to the people of Canada, so long as they did not detract from the value of the road. Mr. Fielding clearly pointed out to the House, that the road would be completed and ready for operation, although at the same time there would be work to be done upon it in the future that would bring it to its ultimate high standard. If that course was open to the commission and it was good railwav business, would the commission be justified in shutting themselves out from that right later on? Were they justified in delivering into the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the keys to the' treasury of this country? Surely * they were the guardians of the money of the people of Canada. If it was in the interest of good railway businesss to adopt this method of building the Transcontinental railway, why should they have shut themselves out of that right by a bargain with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company? Does the hon. gentleman still adhere to the statement that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would refuse to take over the road if there were wooden trestles? Is it not a fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company not only did not so refuse, but encouraged the use of wooden trestles just for the purpose that I have mentioned, and that the Transcontinental Railway Commission, having an eye to the enhancement of the cost, decided against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and built the road without wooden trestles and paid 55 cents a yard for train-haul fills to contractors, thus encouraging the contractors to overbreak and everything else in order to get the 55 cents a yard train-haul fill? I will read the evidence of Mr. Woods, engineer for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. He was examined by the commission and here is what he said on page 432:
Q. Did the Grand Trunk Pacific have anything to do, so far as you know, with the elimination of wooden trestles on the Transcontinental railway ?-A. They did not.
Q. Your company would not have objected to the construction of wooden bridges, as is the usual practice on other new railways in Canada and the United States ?-A. They would not; they even recommended it in some instances.
Q. There are advantages in the construction of wooden bridges on a new railway through a new country, are there not ?-A. There are, in my judgment.
Q. Will you tell us, in your own language, some of the advantages that occur to you ?
In Mr. Woods' answer he shows the various advantages that accrue from wooden bridges. (Reading):
Q. Permanent wooden trestles ?

A. Yes. I think this is generally done in the construction of lines of any magnitude, aside, possibly from Government work here in Canada.
In the face of that evidence, the hon. gentleman tells us that the! company, whose engineer says that they recommended that system of construction to the Transcontinental Railway Commission, who actually tendered themselves and wished to get the contract for filling these wooden trestles at twenty-five cents a yard and

who would thereby have saved millions of dollars to this country, would refuse to take over the road if there were wooden trestles. The hon. gentleman says that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would not take over the road. Is there a portion of the National Transcontinental railway system that is going to be used more than the line between Winnipeg and Fort William, which runs from Winnipeg to Graham, and then by the Grand Trunk Pacific from Superior junction down to Fort William? I think not. Does he tell us that there are no wooden trestles on the line from Graham to Fort William? Why, it is dotted with them. That is the system the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company adopted in building that line in that northern country, a line analogous in every respect to the National Transcontinental railway. If the hon. gentleman will go over this line-I speak now on the authority of one who has been over it-he will find that the road from Graham to Fort William is built in accordance with profiles and the plans; he will find that there is not overbreak to the extent of thirty or forty per cent, as Mr. Macfarlane swears there is allowed on the contract from Graham to Winnipeg. He will find that the excavation there is cut out within reasonable proportions of the original design, and that overbreak is kept down to a minimum through that rough country. But if he looks over the McArthur contract from Graham to Winnipeg, he will find that the road is forty per cent wider than it ought to be; and that overbreak has been indulged in to the extreme. What is the reason? It is because Mr. McArthur was encouraged to indulge in overbreak. He was encouraged to put in dynamite here, there, and everywhere, because on whatever he blew out he got fifty-five cents a yard using it for train-haul fill along the line. Where you have wooden trestles, where you use the system that other railways adopt in railroad building, you do not hold out a prize to the contractors to indulge in the luxury of overbreak. That prize was held out in this case. The engineers of the company, under the compulsion that they themselves have referred to, consented to allow the overbreak that was so thrown down, inasmuch as it was used in train fill. As a consequence, the contractors had a certain right on their side when it came to the arbitration and, as a result, the arbitration board, to which my hon. friend referred, was not in a position to judge of this overbreak qeustion on its own merits. His [Mr. Meigheir..
argument on this overbreak is this: It is true there was some overbreak; it is true there was more overbreak than there should have been; twenty per cent is all that you ordinarily are allowed; there was thirty to forty per cent here, but that is all very well, for we provided an arbitration board to look into that. The arbitration board consisting of Mr. Grant, Mr. Kelleher and Mr. Schreiber, looked into this question and decided that a reduction of $500,000 was all that could be made and that settled the question, and Messrs. Gutelius and Lvnch-Staunton had no further right to interfere in the matter. Does that settle the question? What situation faced the arbitration board? This thing had been going on for years and years. The engineers of the Transcontinental Commission had been passing on this overbreak. Contractors had been encouraged to throw down this great amount of rock, and to make 40 per cent of overbreak instead of 20 per cent, while the rock and clay and loose rock thrown down had been used in the construction of the road instead of trestles. The consequence was, the contractors had rights at this time, which, if the Transcontinental Commission had done its duty, they never would have had. These rights had to be taken into account by the Arbitration Board. But the duty of the investigating commission was to ascertain whether, if the Transcontinental Commission had done its duty, a greater sum would not have been saved in overbreak. And the investigating commissioners found that if the Transcontinental Commission had done its duty, the cost of the reduction in overbreak would not have been merely $500,000 but would have been $678,000 more. The question is not settled by the award of the Arbitration Board. Their finding, doubtless, on the facts before them and with the arguments which the contractors could advance, was a fair finding, I do not challenge that. But the arguments that the contractors could advance would not have 'been possible, they could not have been advanced,	if the	TranscontinentalCommission	had	done its	duty and forbidden this	overbreak.	'Now, the hon. gentleman is very much concerned about the wooden trestles; for, he said, they would no sooner have been built than	the	Railway	Commission of
Canada would have compelled them to be filled up, and the Grand Trunk Pacific would have had to fill theirs up before this if they had been under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission of Canada.

I should like to know what the hon. gentleman's authority is for saying that the Railway Commission of Canada had decided that the wooden trestles had to be filled up. I never heard of such a ruling of the board. If there is a wooden trestle that has had its day and is dangerous to the public, certainly then, as in every other similar case, the Railway Commission would decide that it must be replaced by something safe. But there has been no ruling by the board that wooden trestles are not to be allowed to serve their time on the Transcontinental, the Canadian Pacific, or on any other road. I will read the latest ruling of the commission on the subject, and I will ask the hon. gentleman to point out anything that warrants him in saying that the Railway Commission has set its face against wooden trestles. This was made on the 2nd of August, 1910.
It is ordered and directed:
That every railway company subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, operating by steam power any railway or railways, any part or parts of which is or are constructed of, or upon wooden trestles the whole of which cannot be seen from an approaching train for a distance of at least one thousand feet, do, during the months of May, June, July, August, September and October of each year, provide, place, and keep a watchman, trackwalker, Are alarm signals, ballast flooring, zinc covering over caps and intersections or approved fireproof paint, as hereinafter directed, for the purpose of protecting the said trestles from fire; each such company having the option of adopting any of the said foregoing methods of protection.
This shows that the Railway Commission of Canada has not in any way set its face against wooden trestles, but only insists, in this as in every case, that due precautions shall be taken for the public safety.
