Not only specifically
recognizes them, but directly endorses them. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) imagine that the cost of keeping a man or the cost of having fireproof paint bears any comparison to the saving that would have accrued to the people of Canada if this more sensible and economical manner of constructing the road had been adopted [DOT] in the end resulting in just the road the hon. gentleman says the country set out to secure? What is the interest on about $5,000,000 that this country has lost because the Transcontinental Commission refused to adopt the methods of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway and other roads
in utilizing wooden trestles to secure economical and at the same time thorough construction?
The hon. gentleman tells us that the commissioners' report is entirely wrong also in its conclusion on the Cap Rouge viaduct. The Cap Rouge is a small river, or creek, I understand, that flows into the St. Lawrence between the Quebec bridge and the city of Quebec. In order to cross this they had a steel viaduct which, of course, must have a substructure. In this case the commission saw fit to adopt the character of substructure used in the Quebec bridge, that is, to have the pneumatic caisson instead of the open caisson. As I understand it, in the case of an open caisson, piles are driven until the solid rock is reached, and on the floor formed by the top of these piles, the caisson sits, composed of a wooden structure made up of twelve-by-twelves within which the concrete is built, resulting in a square block of concrete resting securely on the top of the piles. As against this there is the pneumatic caisson, which consists of the concrete being built on the solid rock by means of a pneumatic system of getting air into the enclosure and by keeping out the water, enabling the workmen to work. The hon. gentleman says the commission would never have been justified in using the open caisson on the Cap Rouge viaduct, but had to use the pneumatic caisson such as are used for the substructure of the pillars of the Quebec bridge. He gives as a reason that there was a great depth of mud there, and that the waters of the St. Lawrence come up the Cap Rouge river and reach the viaduct itself, and would have injured the open caisson.
I want to tell the hon. member that not only is there no ground for any such fear in this case, but that he himself is the authority who has proven that there is no such ground. He himself, in case of a viaduct over the Sturgeon river between Graham and lake Superior junction, where the depth and the mud is greater, where the danger is greater,-I am speaking on the authority of engineers who have been there and made an examination-authorized and ratified the use of the open caisson. Not only has he done it at Sturgeon river viaduct, but also in the viaduct over the Vermilion river. In both instances, the very reasons he gave for forbidding the use of open caissons in the Cap Rouge viaduct existed and existed in greater degree -if they are reasons at all. The fact is, there is no such reason, and I speak advis-edly-I speak on the authority of gentlemen

who know-when I say that he cannot point to any instance of this most expensive class of pneumatic caisson in the case of any similar structure on the face of the earth. What is the use of a structure of this kind in the case of the crossing of a little creek or river like the Cap Rouge? The hon. gentleman did not produce any authority whatever for his assertion that there was any danger from the use of open caissons in connection with the Cap Rouge viaduct, and he has failed to justify the conduct of his commission and failed to justify his own conduct in not saving to the people of this country the enormous sum of a quarter of a million dollars that was lost in that regard alone.
I come now to the question of the Chau-diere cut. The hon. gentleman believes that the commission is entirely wrong in this regard also, and that the sum of $351,000, which, it is asserted, might have been saved the country if due regard had been had for economy in connection with that cut would not have been saved. The Chau-difere cut is an expensive one, a mile, I believe, from the extremity of the Quebec bridge. At the Quebec bridge, the hon. gentleman himself admits, there is a one per cent grade, and if only a one per cent grade had been insisted upon in the Chau-diere cut instead of a four-tenths grade, a saving of $351,000 would have been made. If the train is fully loaded, a pusher engine has to be used wherever there is a one per cent grade, but if the train is not fully loaded, a pusher engine is not used. Is it good common sense, therefore, to throw away $351,000 rather than run a pusher engine a mile from the Quebec bridge? Surely that appeals to hon. gentlemen; why not let a pusher engine run a mile from the Quebec bridge, where a pusher engine has to be used on fully-loaded trains? The engineer himself who reported on this matter, and whose advice the hon. gentleman should have followed, said that the prospects for heavy traffic were not such as to warrant the belief that there would be, within a reasonable number of years at all events, any necessity for a pusher engine over the Quebec bridge or over the Chaudiere cut; consequently there was not only a lack of excuse for running a pusher engine out a mile from the bridge, but there was no excuse whatever for throwing away this $351,000 of the public money. It is the same all down the line; it is the same from one end to the other. The pole star set before the Transcontinental Commission seems to have 
been to put all the money they possibly could into the Transcontinental, and then boast about what a fine road they had. If a business concern that has set about to establish, we will isay, a shingle mill, were to insist upon having marble floors, metal roofs, stained glass windows and all other appurtenances which are more fitting in a bank than in a shingle mill, they could justify their course on all fours by the very argument with which hon. gentlemen opposite have attempted to justify the course taken in connection with the Transcontinental railway. The proprietor of the shingle mill could say: We have the best floor in any shingle mill in North America; we have the finest roof to he found in any shingle mill on the continent; we have stained glass windows which are found in no other shingle mill on the continent; we do not need to equate the results so far as profit against capital expenditure is concerned-that is the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite. Even though we are wrong, they say, for goodness' sake do not say so or yon will frighten the financiers of the world. The hon. ex-Minister of Railways has been deeply concerned for the financiers of the world and the reputation of the Grand Trunk Pacific for many years. In 1910, when the terrible state of the financial world that he to-day so vividly depicts and so much deplores did not exist, he had the same fear in his soul that he has now. In 1910, when the then member for Simcoe told the House and told the country and told the world that this Transcontinental railway was going to cost $218,000,000, the hon. gentleman pleaded, for goodness' sake do not say a word about it, or we would frighten the financiers of the world and they would turn their backs upon the Grand Trunk Pacific project. He told them that it was doing an injustice to the Grand Trunk Pacific and doing an injustice to Canada for us to dare say to the financiers of the world that this road was actually going to cost $218,000,000. We were not telling the financiers of the 9 p.m. world the whole truth at that time; we were telling them only part of the truth. On the same basis we know to-day that it will cost $234,000,000 to build the Transcontinental railway. I do not know why in 1910 we would have been justified in taking the advice of the hon. member for South Renfrew and in refusing to tell the financiers of the world even half the truth. I do

not know on what principle we in this House are justified in refusing to disclose the truth about any Canadian project. I do not know that in the end truth does much harm to anybody. The hon. gentleman says it is not the truth, but he says we should not say it, even if it he true. It was not the whole truth in 1910; it was only part of the truth; but so far as it went it was absolutely true, and he was afraid of divulging even that part of the truth. In 1914 he does not want any part of the truth divulged. He says we are wrong in doing so because we are criticising not only the management of this thing but the Government of the day that had control of it as well. Are we to sit in this House and refuse to criticise the Government of that day? When we were in opposition did we criticise it; that was our function as members of the Opposition, and if hon. gentlemen opposite are going to follow the injunction of the hon. member for Renfrew and refuse to criticise the Government of the day for fear of frightening the financiers, had they not better start for home at once? There might have been a Government in power not long age that did not wish the truth to be disclosed about Canadian ventures, either private or public, but that Government went out of power on September 21, 1911. The Gutelius-Staunton report does no injustice to the Grand Trunk Pacific in disclosing the actual facts. The Government of the day does no injustice to them or to anybody else in making known the facts so disclosed, and the Government of the day would be derelict in its duty to the financiers of the world and to Canadian institutions generally if they showed any disposition to withhold in the slightest degree the facts of this or any other case. There is a new ruler in Israel just now, and the facts are going to be disclosed as long as that ruler holds the reins of power.
The hon. gentleman says that the cities of St. John, Halifax and Quebec will be dreadfully alarmed when they hear that there are such things as small momentum grades on the Transcontinental; that they will be fearfully alarmed when they hear that wooden trestles, used on every other railway in the world, are actually used on the Transcontinental, and he calls upon the Prime Minister of the day, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Postmaster General to rise up as three righteous men to save these three cities from the awful catastrophe which will come upon them if the world finds out that momentum grades
and wooden trestles are actually-used on the Transcontinental. I want to assure the hon. member for South Renfrew-I do not need to assure the cities of St. John, Halifax and Quebec; I do not need to assure this country-that the Government of the day can be entrusted to see to the interests of Canadian ports and to the interests of Canadian lines.
The determination of hon. gentlemen opposite to guard so faithfully the interests of Canadian transportation is a determination of very recent growth. It did not have ,an abiding place in their hearts two and a half years ago. It is only two and a half years since they professed utter indifference to the interests of Canadian transportation lines and of Canadian ports. If only they could get some further outlet for the products of western Canada and of Canada' as a whole, they did not care whether it was over American or over Canadian lines. The Government of to-day will see to it that there is no practical degrading whatever, and no diminution of the operating value of the Transcontinental railway by any system of momentum grades or any other system. But at the same time they will see that money is not extracted from the treasury of this country for purely fanciful restilts; and the people of St. John, Halifax and Quebec well know that their interests are secure in the hands of the Government that securely guarded them two and a half years ago, as they have been guarded at all times when such a Government has been in power. They well know that no traffic will be lost to them through any action of this Government in respect of the Transcontinental railway.
Now, Sir, I say in conclusion, the Gutelius-Staunton report stands unmolested and undisturbed by the attack of the hon. gentleman. He has used terms of abuse directed against the authors of that report. I do not think the terms he used were justified. He ,did not apply them to any other man in connection with this whole enterprise. He has turned the vials of his wrath upon them. He has described them in a variety of terms. The same course was followed by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell). But neither of these gentlemen has taken a single finding of that report on the facts: fhe ex-Minister of Railways has not taken p, single assertion in that report or any of the evidence that backed up that assertion, and shown that any of these items which in the report were stated to be possible savings to the people of this country could not have been saved and saved without depreciating in any degree the operating value of that road.

That is the essential finding of that report, that stands and will stand. The $40,000,000 is made up of savings that could have been made without detracting from the operating value of that road, or its value as an asset to the people of Canada; and in that $40,000,000, the $4,500,000 which, in the opinion of Mr. Staunton, was spent illegally is not included. The $40,000,000 includes only that part of the $4,500,000 which was not expended for the Transcontinental Tailway at all, but for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and for which there was no justification whatever. There is $40,000,000 beyond that. Then there are the damages that will be assessed against this country in connection with the northern route into the city of Winnipeg, by reason of the failure of the Government then in power, before they filially determined upon the northern entrance, to come to terms with the Canadian Northern railway, to make a fair bargain with them. These damages are attributable to the mismanagement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham), himself, and of the commission who had charge of this work. These damages are still unknown, but they are estimated by the company injured at $10,000,000. This is not included in the $40,000,000 of savings that the commission say might have been made in the laying out of the line itself, if before that line was laid out, hon. gentlemen opposite had not determined on this rigid and unnecessary adherence to strict rules. A line could have been secured, had the rules been fair and reasonable and more in consonance with the rules adopted by other great railways, which, the commissioners say, would have meant a saving of millions of dollars to this country in addition to the millions mentioned in the report itself.
The responsibility of that is on the hon. member for South Renfrew, but it is in a still greater degree on the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. He is the gentleman who, himself, against the advice of his (Minister of Railways of that day, fathered this institution and foisted it on the people in the form in which it was foisted on them. He is the one primarily responsible, he has proclaimed it as a monument that is to make his name immortal in this country and throughout the world. I think the Gutelius-Staunton report has had this result if it has had no other; it has shown the right hon. leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for South Renfrew that the National Transcontinental railway is not now such a monument as they would

wish to have pressing down upon their remains.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it something of a work of supererogation to discuss this report of Gutelius and Staunton after the very searching and thorough investigation which was made by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He made a speech in tJiis House on which I wish to congratulate him and which, in my opinion, ranks with anything ever heard within the walls of this- Chamber. It dissects that _ report from beginning to end and leaves it standing in all its hideous nakedness. I was much interested to hear the Solicitor General (Mr. M-eighe-n). I saw -some days ago a photograph of that hon. gentleman in one of the Toronto papers and -under it were the words ' the rising hope of the Conservative party,' and I was- anxious t-o hear how high that hope would rise to-night on this great subject. But, Sir, I am free to say that if the Conservative hopes cannot rise higher than that, they will not reach any 'very great height of politioal splendour. The hon. gentleman, just before resuming his seat, said that the object of an opposition was to criticise. Well, Sir, it struck me very forcibly that the Solicitor General thought he was still in opposition. He was continually referring to the hon. member for South Renfrew as the Minister of Railways and Canals, and his whole demeanour was similar to that when he occupied the Opposition benches. His speech was, to my mind, a rather narrow special pleading, without that breadth of argument and that wealth of original suggestion which you would have expected from this rising hope of the Conservative party.
This report has been submitted to members of Parliament and the hon. member for South Renfrew has moved an amendment condemning it. Of that amendment I fully approve.
I say that not from the first to the last page of this report, is there a single earmark of a. desire on the part of these commissioners for an impartial investigation, or to show that they felt their official responsibility. The honourable the Solicitor General says that we complained that Mr. Staunton took part in politics, and he says that- Mr. Staunton had a right to do as he liked. Mr. Staunton was a royal commissioner, appointed by warrant of the Crown to consider of the matters referred to him and to deal impartially and fairly between the parties interested. Is it like

an impartial judge to deliberately step off the bench and announce himself as counsel in the proceedings? That is what Mr. Staunton did. One would have supposed that the royal commissioners investigating a matter of this great importance, touching the honour and integrity of high class business men in this country-the commissioners of the Transcontinental railway- would have said to these gentlemen: 'We are investigating this matter and we are going to take evidence; that evidence may in some measure reflect upon you, and we *will give you the opportunity either to be present when the evidence is taken or to be represented there by counsel.' Did they do that? No. They held a star chamber investigation. They called such witnesses as they liked and when they liked; they took such evidence as suited themselves; they embodied in the record such evidence as suited their purpose and having done that, they toss the report into this parliamentary arena and say:	' On that partial
evidence we base our report of these great wrong-doings.' I say that it was an absolutely partisan investigation; it was not an inquiry by a Royal Commission, but an inquiry, highly paid for by this Government, to find out, if possible, some way of condemning the Transcontinental Commissioners, and I say deliberately that from the beginning to the end of that report theis is not one tittle of evidence to support the findings. It is based on improper evidence and its suggestions and insinuations are insulting to high class business men of this country. What do we find? Take the very first paragraph which has already been dealt with.
Until the appointment of Major R. W. Leonard in the autumn of 1911, no member of the commission had any experience or knowledge of railway building or operation.
It has been said that it was not necessary that the members of the Transcontinental Commission should be experienced railway .men. With that I quite agree. The Minister of Railways and Canals himself i3 not a railway man, yet he is building railways and canals continually. Major Leonard is a very estimable gentleman whom I know exceeding well and I have not a word against him, but it is not unfair to him to say that he never built or operated a railroad in his life and knows no more about operating and building railroads than I or any other man in this country. Why put him up as a paragon of perfection in the construction and operation of railroads?
What further do they say?. The hon. ex-
Minister of Railways and Canals has referred to the last paragraph of the finding in regard to extravagance. Let me refer to another paragraph on page 24. And I submit to this House and to the country that a more slanderous and disgraceful statement never was published by any man, let alone royal commissioners, than is to be found on that page. Every man in this House and every man in the country knows of the late lamented Charles M. Hays. .Every man who knew him knows that no more high-minded man, no man of finer character or greater ability in railway building ever lived in Canada. He was the man that was practically instrumental in starting this great Transcontinental railway. We remember the first speech he made in the Railway Committee in support of this great national undertaking, and it was that .speech practically that influenced the Railway Committee in support of this project. What do these commissioners say?
We unhesitatingly find that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, instead of discountenancing, has rather encouraged this inexperienced commission in its exravagant expenditure on this railway.
If the railway company really expected to operate this railway when completed according to the terms and at the rental provided in its agreement with the Government, we must attribute its want of proper care to its indifference to the interests of its own shareholders or its desire to so increase the cost of construction of the 353 miles of railway, for which it was contractor, so as to reap the largest present profit possible therefrom.
It was a very credulous commission indeed if it relied on its contractor, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, interested as such in high classification, to criticise improper classification where other contractors were concerned, or to expect that that contractor would be astute to discourage expenditures where th ev were the builders of one-seventh of the line.
I say that that statement is a slander .against the Grand Tunk Pacific Railway .Company presided over in England by Mr. Smithers, a man of the highest class, and managed by a board of directors of the highest class in Great Britain, and presided over in this country by the late 0. M. Hays at that time. I want to ask the Prime Minister and the members of his Government if they wish to stand as sponsors for that statement? If they do they have a different feeling in regard to this matter than I believe they have.
I wish to make a few references to the arguments of the hon. Solicitor General in reply to the hon. member for South Renfrew. He spoke of the entrances into Winnipeg and complained that the railway ran

into Winnipeg over a high trestle and on a high embankment. I do not know whether he is in favour of an embankment or not, but I will tell the hon. gentleman this. The embankment is there because the Railway Commissioners of Canada ordered that it should go in on a trestle and that the trestle should be filled. That is the only way you can go in. If the hon. gentleman says you cannot go in on a trestle or an. embankment, he might as well say the Grand Trunk railway, the Canadian Northern railway 'and the Canadian Pacific railway should not go into the city of Toronto on a trestle. The Railway Commissioners ordered them to go in on a railway elevated on a viaduct. In the same way the Transcontinental railway is going into the city of Winnipeg. I have very little to say as to that. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) explained the situation fully. He stated that the Transcontinental railway has the best entrance into the city of Winnipeg. The Solicitor 'General controverts that and says to the contrary. I am willing to let it stand at that without any further word or suggestion from me and I am willing to let these statements go before the people of the 'country for their verdict. I venture to say they will approve of the statement of my non. friend from South Renfrew rather than the statement of the hon. Solicitor General.
Then, we come to another matter that touches us, as far as the Transcontinental railway is concerned, a little more nearly; and that is in connection with the Trans-cona shops. The Solicitor General says tnat Mr. Staunton may very fairly differ from any other legal authorities in the country. The Solicitor General admits that Mr. Lynch-Staunton is wrong in his law.
I do not say that.

Silence gives consent.
His department says so, the Minister of-Justice says so, Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, says so and the Law Clerk says so. If the Solicitor General differs from them and joins Mr. Lynch-Staum-ton, very good for nim. At any rate, he says there is no reason why Mr. Lynch-Staunton should not differ from other legal authorities. There is no reason why he should not. Mr. Lynch-Staunton is a very good lawyer and a very estimable gentleman and I have not a word to say against him. He is a most bitter partisan. I do not believe that in the making of this great world the good Lord ever created a greater

partisan than Mr. George Lynch-Staunton, and I do not believe he ever tried to. But as I have said, he is .an estimable gentleman. It is not the fact that he differs from all the legal authorities that I complain of but it is that he says: in law you should not have built these shops, and because you have built them you nave wasted $4,500,000 of the people's money. If he had said: In law I do not think that you should have built them, but all the other legal authorities are against me; the Minister of Justice, the Deputy Minister of Justice, all the great lawyers in Canada, are against me on the law; Sir William Whyte, the arbitrator, is against me as a matter of practice, and although I think they are all wrong, as I have a right to think so, still, you being right, the expenditure of this money was proper. Why did he not say that? Is that not what a royal commissioner should have said and would have said if he had been a fair royal commissioner? But, no, he said: You are all wrong in law, and being all wrong you have wasted $4,500,000 of the people's money. This expenditure is represented throughout the country as being an extravagant and wasteful expenditure. As a commissioner he should have stated:	I think you are
wrong in law but as you have been held to be right, the money is properly expended.
My hon. friend said something about the cost of the line. We know the cost of the line and we know the cost of other lines. That matter has been fully gone into and it is not necessary for me to weary the House by reiterating these figures. Then he goes on to speak of what we call momentum grades. It would be well to understand just where we are in connection with this matter. There is without doubt much difference of opinion amongst engineers as to whether there should he momentum grades or whether there should be actual grades of 0-4 per cent and 0-6 per cent as provided for. Why has this been done? Why was provision made for a 0 4 per cent grade against eastbound traffic and a 0-6 per cent against westbound traffic and why was it adhered to strictly by the commissioners? Were they right or wrong? It was simply owing to the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific engineers, the engineers of the Railway Commission and the engineers of the Government got together and devised specifications for the construction of this railway and they prepared such specifications and designs as Mr. Hays and the directors of the railway company desired. The board of English directors, represented

toy Mr. Hays in this ountry, said:	We
want a railway built from Winnipeg to Moncton with a grade of 0-4 per cent against eastbound traffic and a grade of 0-6 per cent against westbound traffic; that is the road we will take over and pay rental for, that is the kind of road we expect you to build. That is the kind of road that was intended to be built when they started out and they continued building that kind of a road until this Government began to degrade it. There is the whole question. The *Grand Trunk Pacific built and are building the same class of road west of Winnipeg. They wanted a road from the Atlantic to the Pacific oceans with that kind of grade and they had sufficient knowledge of the country through which this road was running to know that that class of grade could be easily built and without exorbitant cost. It is folly to say that one engineer favours the momentum grade and that another engineer says it is all wrong. I do not care whether it is right or wTong so long as the agreement for the building of the National Transcontinental railway is maintained. That was the policy of the Government. That policy was submitted to the people of Canada in 1904 and received their strong approval. It was submitted to the people in 1908 and again received theiT strong approbation. In 1908, after we had heard in this House, ad nauseum, the same class of talk which has been given us to-night by the Solicitor General against this high class railway, the people approved of it and they will approve of it now.

The hon. gentleman
is mistaken; it was before the 1911 election that these statements were made.

It was not an issue in

It would take the largest hauls of any transcontinental railway on the American continent. My hon. friend the Solicitor General, speaking of grades, said it was impossible for ninety-seven cars to be hauled in one train. He is wrong. There is a railroad in Canada to-day that hauls not only ninety-seven cars, but one hundred cars or more.
One hundred and twenty cars.

Yes, one hundred and
twenty oars, and that road is the Michigan Central railroad.
Loaded cars?

Loaded	cars. I have
counted them time and again.

How	did you knew

They are sealed and I
presume they are loaded. In going from Chicago to New York these trains pass the town of Welland in which I live. On the Canada .southern division of the Michigan Central there are just the same gradients that there will be on this National Transcontinental railway.
My hon. friend says that the Canadian Pacific railway have momentum grades. I presume they have. I believe that every railroad, in its initial operations, as a rule establishes these momentum grades to some extent in order to cheapen the cost of construction. The grades are taken out later on as time progresses and as circumstances warrant.
These have been put in just lately in the revision of the road.

I quite appreciate that
fact, but it is to get rid of one per cent grades, which are much heavier grades than these momentum grades are.
To get over the hump.

I know pretty well about the Canadian Pacific railway west of Winnipeg, although perhaps not as much as does the Solicitor General. I know that the Canadian Pacific railway west of Winnipeg has been totally rebuilt, at least once and probably more than once. Which would be the cheaper, to build a first-class road in the beginning or to build a second-class road and then in a few years rebuild it? The question really comes down to that. Mr. Hays, the directors and the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway company thought that it would be better for them, in order to carry the great traffic which they anticipated they would get right from the start, to have a first-class road built immediately and that they would rather undertake to pay the interest on the cost of construction of a first-class road from the start than to have a second-class road from the start which would debar them from hauling the freight which they

expected to get and which they intended to go after. Consequently, they said: Build a first-class road and we will take the responsibility of paying the interest on it. Who will find fault with them for doing so? The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) last night rather insinuated that the Grand Trunk Pacific would never take over this road. They will never take it over if this Government degrades it so that they cannot carry the freight they expect to obtain. If the road is kept up to the standard at which it was maintained until this Government came into power, there is no doubt as to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company taking it over.
My hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) spoke rather derogatorily of the capitalization and of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I would like to tell him and this House and the country that, in the Act confirming the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company we find that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, one of the wealthiest institutions of America, is behind this project; that it is compelled to take a large percentage of the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific and hold it during the whole term of this lease, namely, fifty years. This company is bound to guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the cost of construction over and above the bonds guaranteed by the Government. Therefore the Grand Trunk Railway Company are behind the carrying out of the agreement made by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. My hon. friend, forsooth, presumes to insinuate that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, composed of men of the highest class men in Great Britain, is endeavouring to keep up expenditure in the construction of this road so as to have an excuse to violate the terms of the contract. That seems to me to be absolutely and utterly absurd. Yet Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton say that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have no idea of economy, and that they are trying to make a few paltry dollars out of their contracts for the construction of this railway. Everyone who knows anything about the matter knows why the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company entered into the field as competitors for the work. They made their reason absolutely plain at the time. They said: We will likewise go into the field as competitors so as to keep down the prices on these contracts; we will see what the work is going to cost and will bid ourselves and, 
if we cannot get the appliances to build the railway, we will sublet the work to other contractors at our prices and will see that the road is built at the proper figure and on economical principles. That is why they went into the construction. I presume they are quite satisfied to make the few dollars they would make just as any other contractor would be, but their primary object was to keep down the cost of construction.
My hon. friend says that momentum grades do not degrade the road. They make it more difficult for locomotives to haul trains over the road, as heavy trains cannot be hauled over a road with momentum grades as can be hauled over a level road. The primary object of every railway company on the American continent is so to reduce the grades of their line that they can haul the heaviest possible trains. The Grand Trunk Railway Company did that; the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is doing it too. Every railroad in the United States is doing it because they are compelled to do it in order to compete with the water routes in the hauling of freight. They are all the time bringing down their gradients to the lowest possible figure. Although a momentum grade may not so seriously degrade the road as to make it unfit for use, of course the company can haul the freight, but they cannot haul the quantity of freight and they cannot haul it at as low a figure.
My hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) says that he has never heard of Mr. Berry. My hon. friend is young yet. He will probably hear of Mr. Berry lateT on. He has heard of him at any rate in this discussion. I have heard of Mr. Berry and can corroborate what the hon. member for South Renfrew has said, that he is the highest railway authority on the American continent. What he does not know about railroad construction, about gradients and about the classification of a railway for freight haulage, there is very little use of any man in this country endeavouring to find out. What he says I fully and heartily rely on.
My hon. friend also spoke about the curvatures and the trestles. As to the trestles, I might say this. He read the evidence of Mr. Woods that the Grand Trunk Railway Company was willing that wooden trestles should be put in. What is the position?
They were willing they should be put in if the Grand Trunk Pacific were allowed to fill them in after, and thereby delay the operation of the lease for a couple of years and lose to this country 3 per cent a year

on the total cost of construction. They said: We will not take over the road as a going concern if wooden trestles are built, but we will fill them in and hold back the rental for that length of time. What would these hon. gentlemen opposite have said if that had been done? What a howl of indignation we should have heard from the Solicitor General then. He would have said: Why did you not carry out your agreement and build a first-class road?
In regard to curvatures the position is exactly the same. These matters were settled, as I have already said, between the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, through Mr. Hays, representing the English board of directors, the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the engineers of the Commission and the engineers of the Government. The class of railway then decided upon is the class of railway they set out to build, and that is the class of railway which should have been built without any degradation. To show that that was the intention, to show that that was the object of the Grand Trunk Pacific company, just so soon as this Government attempted to degrade the road by putting in momentum grades, they got a letter from Mr. Chamberlin, President of the Grand Trunk Pacific, saying: You are degrading the road, and we will not take it over. He immediately repudiates the proposition; he palls the attention of the Railway Commissioner, Major Leonard, this great railway builder, to the fact that the road is being degraded and the agreement entered into violated, and declares that if this continues the company will not feel bound to take over the road. And that letter stands there to-day a menace to this Government or to any Government in regard to the taking over of that road by the Grand Trunk Pacific. When you have it finished next year, ready to put trains on it and you say to the Grand Trunk Pacific: There is the road completed-his answer will be:	There is	my letter	written
two years ago	in which I pointed
out that you had degraded the road; and you have admitted through your Solicitor General in the House of Commons that that is the effect of your action, why, then, should we be compelled to take over the road? Has not the hon. gentleman placed in the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific solicitors the greatest brief that they could hold for the maintenance of their case? The Government have violated the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific and will continue violating it unless they cease putting in
momentum grades and get back to the situation which existed prior to the time when the former Commissioners were turned out.
While the hon. gentleman is on that point, will he be good enough to read the portion of the agreement that prevents the putting in of wooden trestles or momentum grades?

The whole thing was
approved of-
Read the clause of the agreement.
Go on with your argument; I will find it.

Now, the Solicitor General says that by reason of the exdVlinister of Railways having refused to make these changes, the country has lost $6,200,000. I defy him to find within the four comers of this evidence one iota of testimony to justify his statement.
Why did not the hon. gentleman ask me while I was speaking and had the evidence before me?
The hon. gentleman has the evidence before him.
No, I have not it now.

There is nothing to show that the country lost that money by reason of the ex-Minister of Railways refusing to change these grades. We have engineers saying that money would have been saved if momentum grades had been put in. They express themselves sometimes in percentages and sometime? otherwise. But they have shown what the whole object of this proposition was-a high-class road built as speedily as possible. We find that provided for in sections 42 and 43 of this agreement. And, Sir, it seems to me that the reading of these sections is sufficient to justify not only the conduct of the old 'Commissioners but also that of the old Government in what they did, and enough to justify this Government in turning at once back to the standard which the old Government had set:
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the Government

of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports.
How in the name of all that is sensible could the Grand Trunk Pacific, having a longer haul to carry the products of the Northwest to the Atlantic than the American lines have, secure traffic unless they have & railway of the highest possible standard? I say, that ishows in itself the reason why this road was to be of high-class. The Act further says:
The company further agrees that it shall not in any matter within its power directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight hy routes other than those above approved and shall in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
Is that not itself a sufficient answer to the special pleading of the hon. Solicitor General? I submit that it is a plain answer to his suggestion with regard to the construction of this road. In ordeT to haul freight as cheaply as it could he hauled over shorter routes, a high-class road had to be built, and the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific asserted to the . former Government: Yon build us that class of road; we will take it ovct and operate it on the rentals which he have suggested, and we will build up a through Canadian traffic which will develop your ocean ports, build up your great northern country and develop the whole of Canada. My hon. friend says that tlhe railway will not get the traffic. I am loath to heaT these little Canadians talk in the 'Canadian House of Commons. Many years ago, when the Canadian Pacific railway was being built, we heard the Conservatives shouting for a greater Canada: the products of the West would come teeming down to the Bast; the products from the old land would go forth to the West oveT this great transcontinental railway, and Canada would he built up and become a hive of industry through their magnificent diplomacy and their energetic endeavour. But when a Liberal Government comes

along and begins the establishment of a new transcontinental railway, better in construction, running through a far better country, leading directly to Canadian seaports, these little Canadian Tories stand up and say: When you have built the road you will get no traffic; you will be unable to pay interest on the money; the Grand Trunk Pacific railway will not get traffic enough to pay the Government the amount of rental provided in the lease, and the whole thing will be a failure. I regret very much to hear that sentiment expressed at this day in His Majesty's House of Commons. I have greater faith in Canada than that. So far as the normern part of the province of Ontario is concerned, it will not be seven years, it will not be five years, before a profitable local traffic will be developed on that line 'which will go a long way towards paying the rental provided for in that agreement. cannot say that momentum grades or wooden trestles are debarred by the specifications.

Mr. Chamberlin says

the specifications; I am reading from the statute authorizing the making of the specifications.

My friend the Solicitor
General will have to revise his legal opinions; he had better consult his friend, Mr. Lynch-Staunton.

In regard to the traffic, the hon. member for South Renfrew said that according to Mr. Tye, 8-05
10 p.m. trains both ways each day would develop a traffic and an income sufficient not only to pay all the working expenses and the rental provided for in the agreement, but to leave a fair margin of profit as well. You will have to
change the Government first.

the Government will be changed the very first time the people of the country are given an opportunity to do it, particularly when they thoroughly understand what the Government is doing in regard to this great national undertaking which they approved on two different occasions.
This country is big enough to maintain three transcontinental railways, and the Grand Trunk Pacific, being the best, will get the traffic. I do not wonder that the Canadian Pacific railway take a little umbrage at the high-class construction of the Transcontinental railway. I have heard men say, first-class engineers and leading railway men, that when the Grand Trunk Pacific railway is completed and in opera-136
tion, the Canadian Pacific railway will have to rebuild their line in order to compete with the Grand Trunk Pacific-and they are doing it now. They will have to rebuild their line and bring down their grades; any man who knows anything about railroad operation-and I know a little about it by reason of having talked to prominent railway men-knows that the railroad Which has the low grades gets the business and the railroad that has the high grades does not. My hon. friend dealt with the question of tenders, and in that connection I wish to make a reference or two to this precious document of Gutelius and Staunton, which says:
The rules adopted by the commission in advertising- for tenders, the unlimited security required to be furnished by the contractors, and the proposal to let the work for the most part in unreasonably large sections, resulted in only live contractors tendering for S06 miles of the railway, and eleven contracting firms secured all the work and sub-let it to upwards of 100 sub-contractors, who, had the work been divided into reasonably large sections and the security required in other governmental contracts only been exacted, would have in all probability competed in the bidding. As ah indication of the handsome profits derived by these eleven firms, it appears that they were paid $8,800,000 in profits for that part of their work which they let to sub-contractors.
They say that by making smaller sections a greater number of bids would have been put in and there would have been keener competition. I have heard that said in this House. There is no large work undertaken in this day of the world which is let out in small sections; that is a thing of the past, when work was done by horses and scrapers and ploughs and shovels and picks and wheelbarrows and wagons. Then you would let out work in small sections. But now,' when the work is done by means of steam shovels, steam drills and steam derricks, big sections have to be advertised. Why? Because the cost of the plant is so enormous that unless a contractor is offered a big section he will not bid, he will not take a small section. A contractor must have a section big enough to allow him to pay for his plant at least. The Welland canal has been referred to. I know something about that. I remember that when the present Welland canal was built, it was let out in small sections and hundreds of contractors were at work up and down the canal, many of them failing continually, and the Government was in trouble all the time with small contractors. What happens now? They are building a new ship canal with thirty-foot draft and enormous



locks, a canal which it is estimated will cost $50,000,000. It is divided into nine sections of an average of a little over $5,000,000 a section. There is one section, it is true, which is a very short one, only a mile in length, in which the work will cost $10,000,000. That had to be let in one section. There will be another section or two which will be short, but will cost a large amount of money. The average is over $5,000,000. What happened? Every small contractor in western Canada, yes, in the whole of Canada, began to inquire how the work was to be let, whether in small or large sections. Many of them came to me, and I inquired from Mr. Weller, chief engineer of the canal, what was going to be done. He said: I am certainly going to let that work in sections large enough to permit the contractor to pay for his plant at least during the course of construction. And so he has done. There was a great howl. The Minister of Railways had considerable trouble with his own party friends, who endeavoured to force him to have Mr. Weller divide this up into smaller sections so that smaller men could get the jobs. Mr. Weller said no, and Mr. Cochrane, the Minister of Railways and Canals, very properly backed him up in that and said it must be let in big sections so as to secure as prompt a construction of that work as possible. That is the only way in which a great work of that kind can be accomplished. That work is being let in nine sections. Only four contracts have been let but the sub-letting is going on now and always will. No large work has been done without sub-contracting. Take the Erie canal from Buffalo to Albany. My hon. friend the Solicitor General said that a large amount of money was lost on the Cap Rouge viaduct. If he would read the evidence of Mr. M. P. Davis, he would see the whole cause of the difficulty. Cap Rouge is a neck of the river. There is tidal water there; the water rises from sixteen to eighteen feet. 
There is a mud bottom. The contractors were to put in that tidal water a concrete foundation. The engineer of the commission and the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific decided that piles should be driven and an open caisson built on those piles. Messrs. M. P. and J. P. Davis got the contract and went down there to look over the work. In	his
evidence, Mr. M. P. Davis said:	I

When the engineers discussed the matter with him, he said that they should build the foundation using a pneumatic caisson. Mr. M. P. Davis is an expert on pneumatic caissons, one of the best in America and certainly the best in Canada. After the engineers of the commission and the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific had discussed the matter together, they decided that a pneumatic caisson was required. They built the pneumatic caisson and that is what made the extra expense. Yet Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton criticised the commission for adopting the suggestions of engineers who knew fully as much as Mr. Gutelius and very much more than Mr. Lynch-Staunton in that regard.

And what further insinuations are made against Mr. Parent? In contract 8 with M. P. Davis and Company, there was a question of timber price. Mr. Davis put it in at $80 a thousand feet. And he says: I put that in because I believed that on timber delivered in that country it is a proper price. These commissioners insinuate that Mr. Parent, the chairman of the commission, changed the date of the document from the 8th to the 18th of October to show that the document had been signed subsequent to the putting in of this timber price. And be was asked the question and his reply was: It may have been changed, but if so, it was changed since I gave up the chairmanship of that commission. And that is the class of insinuation that runs throughout the whole length of this so-called report of Royal Commissioners, men appointed to investigate and hold the scales of justice even as between the Transcontinental Commissioners and the people of Canada. Can any man say that a report of that kind is justified by the evidence? I say, no; any man who reads the evidence must come to the conclusion that it is a garbled statement got up for a special purpose of a partisan character, to discredit a political party, and, if possible, to injure one of the greatest industrial enterprises ever established in Canada.
